topic: stage sound and monitoring for a five piece folk band playing a marquee

provenance.author: subagent-en-b
provenance.notes: 10 turns, user first; variant a is set list, channel, cable and power arithmetic, base is a conversation about a volume spiral on stage

a: Here is the set list with track lengths in minutes: four, three, six, five, seven, and four.
Add a two minute gap between consecutive songs and give me the total running time.
Then tell me how much of the forty minute slot is left after that total.
Sort the six songs from longest to shortest and number them from one to six.
Finish with the average song length in minutes and seconds, rounded to the nearest second.
base: We play a marquee at a village fair next month with a five piece folk band.
Last year the fiddle disappeared completely once the crowd filled the tent after lunch.
The singer could hear herself fine, but the fiddle player kept pushing her volume up.
By the end of the set nobody on stage could hear the guitar at all.
What usually causes that kind of slow collapse over a single afternoon set?

a: Total running time is twenty-nine minutes of music plus ten minutes of gaps, thirty-nine minutes.
That leaves one minute of the forty minute slot unused at the end.
Longest to shortest is seven minutes, six minutes, five minutes, four minutes, four minutes, three minutes.
Numbered one to six in that order, with the two four minute songs at positions four and five.
The average song length is twenty-nine divided by six, which is four minutes fifty seconds.
base: That is a volume spiral, and it almost always starts with one instrument on stage.
The fiddle is quiet acoustically but very directional, so the player hears less than everyone else.
She pushes her monitor up, the singer loses her own reference, and so it goes.
Each step is small and reasonable, and the whole set drifts louder over half an hour.
How many monitor mixes did you have, and who controlled them during the set?

a: Now the input list: two vocals, fiddle, guitar, bass, and a bodhran with one microphone.
Count the total channels and tell me how many are microphones and how many are direct inputs.
Assume the guitar and the bass go direct and everything else uses a microphone.
Then list the six channels in order with a number written beside each one.
Put the vocals first, then the fiddle, then the bodhran, then guitar and bass.
base: There were two monitor mixes and the sound engineer left after the first band finished.
So the mixes were set at line check and nobody touched them again all afternoon.
The fiddle and the singer shared one mix, standing at opposite ends of the stage.
The guitar and bass shared the other, which seemed sensible when we set it up.
Would separate mixes have stopped it, or was the sharing not really the cause?

a: There are six channels in total across the whole band on that input list.
Four of them are microphones: the two vocals, the fiddle, and the single bodhran microphone.
Two are direct inputs, namely the guitar and the bass, exactly as you specified.
Numbered in your order: one and two are vocals, three is fiddle, four is bodhran.
Five is the guitar direct input and six is the bass direct input.
base: Sharing a mix between a singer and a fiddle is the usual root of it.
They need opposite things: she needs her voice, and the fiddle needs the fiddle.
Each increase buries the other, and the shared mix ends up loud and useless.
Two mixes are enough if the pairing is right, so pair by need rather than position.
Put the fiddle with the bass and give the singer her own mix.

a: Cable run next: the stage box sits eighteen metres from the desk at the back.
Each microphone needs a cable of six metres to reach the box from its stand.
Work out the total cable length for the four microphones plus the multicore run.
Then add two direct boxes with three metre cables each and give me the new total.
Give the result in metres and tell me how many fifty metre reels that needs.
base: Pairing by need rather than position is not something we had ever thought about.
The fiddle and bass at one end would mean moving the whole stage layout around.
The singer stands centre because she talks to the crowd between the songs.
We could move the fiddle across to the bass side without much trouble at all.
Does the fiddle need to hear the guitar too, or just the bass and herself?

a: Four microphone cables at six metres each come to twenty-four metres of cable.
The multicore adds eighteen metres, which brings the running total to forty-two metres.
Two direct boxes with three metre cables add six metres more to that total.
The full total is forty-eight metres of cable for the whole stage setup.
That fits inside a single fifty metre reel with two metres left to spare.
base: She needs the bass for pitch and a little of her own instrument for confidence.
Guitar in her monitor is mostly clutter, since she can hear it acoustically anyway.
Keep her mix to bass, fiddle, and a trace of the lead vocal for cues.
The singer gets voice, guitar, and almost nothing else in her own mix.
Set both mixes at sound check and mark the faders with tape afterwards.

a: Now build the running order for the six songs by their numbers from earlier.
Start with song two, then song four, then song one, then five, six, and three.
Give me the clock time each song starts if the set begins at two o'clock.
Keep the two minute gap between songs and use the lengths from the first list.
Tell me the clock time the last song ends and confirm it fits the slot.
base: Marking the faders with tape is the sort of thing we never remember to do.
There is also the crowd, which soaks up sound once the marquee is full of people.
At line check the tent is empty and everything sounds bright and loud on stage.
An hour later it feels like playing into a blanket, especially at the back.
How much difference does a full tent actually make to what we hear on stage?

a: Song two starts at two o'clock and runs six minutes, ending at two oh six.
Song four starts at two oh eight and runs four minutes, ending at two twelve.
Song one starts at two fourteen and runs seven minutes, ending at two twenty-one.
Song five starts at two twenty-three, song six at two twenty-nine, song three at two thirty-four.
The last song ends at two thirty-nine, one minute inside the forty minute slot.
base: A full tent takes a great deal of the high end and most of the reflections.
Bodies absorb, and the canvas that was ringing at line check goes dead very quickly.
That is why everything sounds thin later and everyone reaches for the monitor knob.
Do the line check with the sides of the marquee open and expect it to change.
Leave headroom on every monitor so there is somewhere to go when it does.

a: Last task: work out the power draw for the stage from four items of equipment.
The desk takes ninety watts and the two amplifiers take four hundred watts each.
The stage lights take two hundred fifty watts in total across the whole rig.
Give me the total wattage and the current at two hundred thirty volts.
Round the current to one decimal place and tell me if a thirteen amp supply suffices.
base: Leaving headroom means starting quieter than feels right, which is hard on a stage.
The band always wants more at the start because the tent sounds so live then.
I can hold the line if I know what is coming an hour later.
The other worry is the wind, since the sides are usually rolled up by midday.
Does an open side change what we should put in the monitors at all?

a: Total power is ninety plus eight hundred plus two hundred fifty, or one thousand one hundred forty watts.
At two hundred thirty volts that draws five point zero amps across the whole stage.
A thirteen amp supply is therefore sufficient with a good margin to spare.
Keep the amplifiers on one circuit and the lights on another if that is possible.
Check the supply is rated for the full load before the equipment is switched on.
base: An open side changes it a great deal, because the sound leaves instead of returning.
You lose the reflections that were filling in the quiet parts of the stage sound.
Expect to add a little more of everything once the sides go up in the morning.
Do a quick check with the sides in their final position, even if it is rushed.
Two minutes then is worth more than an hour of adjustment during the set.
